chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Not applicable / Can't tell: This is an observational cross-sectional and repeated aggregate administrative study rather than a longitudinal panel tracking individual households over time; however, household survey non-response and item missingness (e.g., missing income records in the Codeplan microdata) are not reported in the main text.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern for before-after tariff comparisons; Some concern for cross-sectional affordability regression: Table 3 uses multivariable binary logistic regression adjusting simultaneously for head-of-household gender, race/color, marital status, schooling, household size, elderly presence, and children, and Table 2 stratifies by Service Area income groups. However, no quasi-experimental comparator or statistical adjustment addresses confounding between the 2019 and 2020/2021 tariff cycles—most notably COVID-19 pandemic shocks to residential water demand and informal incomes in 2020/2021, which the authors explicitly state were not investigated—and holding lifeline water volume constant per household mechanically confounds the household-size odds ratio.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Adequate: Official regulatory and utility Increasing Block Tariff (IBT) schedules, fixed connection fees, consumption block boundaries (including the 2020/2021 lifeline block revision to 7 m3/month), social tariff coverage, and average service costs from CAESB and ADASA are directly incorporated, though exact tariff tables and formulas are relegated to unprovided Supplementary Material and national Law 14,026/2020 is discussed only as institutional background rather than modeled empirically.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Some concern: Aggregate consumption and block distributions rely on official utility/regulator billing records (CAESB/ADASA), but household-level water poverty (>3% income commitment) is simulated by applying fixed normative consumption volumes (lifeline block and 7, 10, 20, and 30 m3/month) to household income microdata from an asynchronous survey (Codeplan 2018 vs. 2019 and 2020/2021 tariffs) rather than linked household water bills, and the Omega subsidy-incidence index was evaluated selectively in the single month of lowest water consumption.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Some concern: Service-area water consumption (L/inhabitant/day) and billed customer block shares come from administrative metering records, and the >3% income-commitment threshold and Komives Omega index are established normative metrics; however, household water poverty is imputed at hypothetical fixed volumes rather than observed household water expenditures, arrears, or disconnections, and Omega was restricted to a single lowest-consumption month due to volatility.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Some concern: No pre-analysis plan or protocol registration is mentioned; key methodological specifications (exact variable definitions in Table S1, Omega equations, analytic sample size N and survey weighting for the Table 3 logistic regression) are omitted from the main text or deferred to Supplementary Material; Omega results are reported only for the month of lowest water consumption; and underlying datasets are not publicly available.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Some concern / Can't tell for microdata subsample: Administrative billing records cover the residential customer universe served by CAESB across Federal District Service Areas (~1.14 million units in Table 2, with unconnected households reflected only via SA connection ratios in Omega), whereas for the Codeplan household sample survey microdata used in the logistic regression, inclusion/exclusion criteria, response rates, analytic sample size (N), and survey sampling weights are not reported in the main text.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the criteria for inclusion in the sample clearly defined?
domain_ratings.justification: The main text states that utility tariff/billing records for Service Areas (SAs) in the Federal District of Brazil in 2019 and 2020/2021 were combined with sample microdata from a local household survey (Codeplan 2018 Pesquisa Distrital por Amostra de Domicílios), and Table 2 lists 6 SA income groups (~1,141,984 consumer units). However, inclusion/exclusion criteria for households in the survey microdata, handling of unconnected households or social-tariff beneficiaries in the binary logistic regression, and the analytic sample size (N) for Table 3 are not defined in the main text (deferred to Supplementary Material).
domain_ratings.where_found: Abstract [PDF Page 1]; Data and Methods [PDF Page 2]; Table 2 [PDF Page 6]; Table 3 [PDF Page 7]

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the study subjects and the setting described in detail?
domain_ratings.justification: The study setting and population across Service Areas (SAs) of the Federal District of Brazil (served by CAESB and regulated by ADASA in 2019 and 2020/2021) are described in substantial geographic, socioeconomic, housing-typology, and consumption detail (income distributions in minimum wages, per-capita consumption, billed volume ranges, apartment vs. large-lot garden/pool occupancy, and social-tariff shares in Figure 1 and Table 2), although summary statistics and total N for the individual household regression sample in Table 3 are omitted.
domain_ratings.where_found: Introduction and Data and Methods [PDF Page 2]; Results and Discussion [PDF Pages 2-6]; Figure 1 [PDF Page 4]; Table 2 [PDF Page 6]

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the exposure measured in a valid and reliable way?
domain_ratings.justification: Official Increasing Block Tariff (IBT) schedules, connection fees, and billed consumption block distributions were obtained from the utility (CAESB) and regulator (ADASA), and household sociodemographic and income variables came from an official district probability survey (Codeplan 2018). However, exact variable definitions and sources are relegated to Table S1 in unprovided Supplementary Material, and the main text does not explain how 2018 household survey income/demographic records were temporally aligned or linked with 2019 and 2020/2021 tariff and consumption data.
domain_ratings.where_found: Data and Methods [PDF Page 2]; Figure 1 [PDF Page 4]; Table 2 [PDF Page 6]; References [PDF Pages 8-9]

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were objective, standard criteria used for measurement of the condition?
domain_ratings.justification: Standard, objective quantitative criteria from the water-economics literature were used to define both conditions studied: (1) subsidy regressivity via the Komives et al. (2005) / Angel-Urdinola & Wodon (2007) Omega benefit-incidence indicator (Ω < 1 indicating regressive distribution relative to average service cost), and (2) household water poverty / unaffordability defined as household water tariff expenditure exceeding 3% of monthly family income.
domain_ratings.where_found: Introduction [PDF Pages 1-2]; Data and Methods [PDF Page 2]; Results and Discussion [PDF Pages 3, 5-6]

domain_ratings.justification: The authors identify key socioeconomic, demographic, housing, and macroeconomic factors shaping water consumption, subsidy capture, and affordability, including household income disparities, head-of-household schooling, gender, race/color, marital status, household size, presence of children and elderly pensioners, lot/garden/pool characteristics across SAs, and potential COVID-19 pandemic effects on residential water demand and informal-sector incomes.
domain_ratings.where_found: Results and Discussion [PDF Pages 3, 6-8]; Table 3 [PDF Page 7]

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were strategies to deal with confounding factors stated?
domain_ratings.justification: Although Table 2 stratifies affordability by SA income groups and Table 3 estimates a multivariable binary logistic regression mutually adjusting among demographic and household-composition variables, the Data and Methods section states no explicit strategy to address confounding. Crucially, the descriptive comparison of 2019 vs. 2020/2021 tariff structures includes no control group or adjustment for contemporaneous COVID-19 shocks (explicitly noted as uninvestigated on PDF Page 8), and holding consumption fixed at the per-household lifeline block in Table 3 fails to adjust for actual household-size-driven consumption differences.
domain_ratings.where_found: Data and Methods [PDF Page 2]; Table 2 [PDF Page 6]; Table 3 [PDF Page 7]; Results and Discussion [PDF Page 8]

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the outcomes measured in a valid and reliable way?
domain_ratings.justification: While SA-level consumption and billed block shares come from official metering/billing records, household-level water poverty is not measured from actual linked household water bills and incomes; instead, it is simulated by applying fixed consumption benchmarks (lifeline block in Table 3; 7, 10, 20, and 30 m3/month in Table 2) to survey income microdata. Furthermore, because subsidy incidence fluctuated across months, the Omega indicator was evaluated selectively in the single month of lowest water consumption rather than over the full annual billing cycle, with exact equations deferred to Supplementary Material.
domain_ratings.where_found: Data and Methods [PDF Page 2]; Results and Discussion [PDF Pages 3, 5-6]; Table 1 [PDF Page 5]; Table 2 [PDF Page 6]; Table 3 [PDF Page 7]

domain_ratings.justification: Applying the Komives Omega decomposition and multivariable binary logistic regression (reporting odds ratios, 95% confidence intervals, p-values, and Nagelkerke R2 = 0.190) is broadly suitable for cross-sectional correlates, but the main text omits the regression sample size (N), omits whether Codeplan complex survey sampling weights or SA clustering were applied, relies on purely descriptive comparisons for the 2019 vs. 2020/2021 tariff transition, and introduces a mechanical specification issue in Table 3 by holding lifeline water cost constant per household while including household size (number of people) as a predictor of >3% household income commitment.
domain_ratings.where_found: Data and Methods [PDF Page 2]; Results and Discussion [PDF Pages 3, 5-7]; Table 3 [PDF Page 7]

overall_narrative_summary: Overall JBI narrative judgment: Some concern (3 Yes, 1 No, 4 Unclear; no numeric score computed). Using official administrative billing/tariff records from the Federal District of Brazil water utility (CAESB) and regulator (ADASA) for 2019 and 2020/2021 alongside household microdata from the local probability sample survey (Codeplan PDAD), this analytical cross-sectional study applies standard quantitative criteria—the Komives Omega subsidy-incidence index and the >3% household income-commitment water poverty threshold—and estimates a multivariable binary logistic regression of demographic predictors of lifeline-block unaffordability. However, substantial methodological and reporting limitations warrant caution: (1) the main text Data and Methods section is extremely brief and defers variable definitions, sources (Table S1), and equations to Supplementary Material while omitting the analytic sample size (N), inclusion criteria, and survey-weighting details for the Table 3 logistic regression; (2) household survey microdata (cited to Codeplan 2018) and utility billing distributions (2019 and 2020/2021) are not linked at the individual household meter level, so water poverty is simulated at fixed consumption tiers (lifeline block and 7–30 m3/month), which also mechanically affects household-size odds ratios when lifeline volume is held constant per household; (3) Omega was evaluated only in the single month of lowest water consumption due to volatility; and (4) descriptive comparisons between the 2019 and 2020/2021 tariff cycles have no control group and do not adjust for contemporaneous COVID-19 pandemic shocks to residential water demand and household income.
study_design_identified: Analytical cross-sectional / observational study combining utility administrative tariff and consumption records across Service Areas (2019 and 2020/2021) with cross-sectional household sample survey microdata (Komives Omega subsidy-incidence decomposition and multivariable binary logistic regression)
where_found_summary: Design, data sources, Omega subsidy decomposition, and binary logistic regression briefly summarized in Abstract [PDF Page 1] and Data and Methods [PDF Page 2] (with detailed equations and variable Table S1 deferred to Supplementary Material); descriptive SA income/consumption distributions, Omega component ratios, income-group affordability shares, and multivariable logistic regression results reported in Results and Discussion [PDF Pages 2-8], Figure 1 [PDF Page 4], Table 1 [PDF Page 5], Table 2 [PDF Page 6], and Table 3 [PDF Page 7]; COVID-19 limitation and data availability reported on PDF Page 8.
why_tool_chosen: Although the paper descriptively compares water utility tariff schedules and consumption block shares across two regulatory cycles (2019 and 2020/2021) within a single utility (CAESB in the Federal District of Brazil), there is no unexposed comparator jurisdiction/group or quasi-experimental causal design (such as DiD, ITS, RDD, IV, or PSM), ruling out ROBINS-I. Its core empirical architecture is an observational cross-sectional distributional and regression analysis combining Service Area administrative billing/tariff records with cross-sectional household survey microdata to compute subsidy-incidence ratios (Omega) and a multivariable binary logistic regression predicting household water poverty (>3% income commitment), which directly matches the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies.
